analysis.title: 2026 Midterm Election Recap: Weekly Recap, Taking stock of the post-election results and major market moves
key_insights: Democrats won the Nov 2026 midterms by a wider margin than expected, especially in the Senate and governor races. In the Senate they held all 13 legacy seats and flipped 7 Republican seats, for 54 Democratic seats vs 44 Republican. Alaska and Mississippi are close and could add 2 more.

The House went largely as polls expected: 253 Democratic seats vs 162 Republican, with 20 races still uncalled. Neither party has a supermajority. Five governorships flipped to Democrat, including Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Nevada and Texas.

The report compares the result to the 1974 and 2006 midterms. Stocks were in a bear market in 1974 and the Global Financial Crisis was close in 2006. Today equity and credit markets have outperformed for years and sit at stretched valuations.

Foreign policy: it is unclear whether strikes on Iran stop or intensify before the new Congress sits. Oil is falling on news of a potentially new Defense Secretary, which suggests the former. The report is skeptical that a complete resolution to the war is imminent.

Business investment: a Democratic Congress is expected to bring more aggressive oversight of AI. Speculative AI investment could slow, and new regulation will likely take months or years. Democratic governors could slow data center construction. The added AI uncertainty is a headwind to growth and investment.

Fiscal: divided government raises the hurdle for new discretionary spending, especially in early 2027. A continuing resolution must pass to fund the government by Dec 11. Raising the debt ceiling is the largest medium-term risk. Mandatory programs and interest costs keep pushing outlays higher despite gridlock.

Possible compromise areas are prescription drugs and healthcare and EV credits. Tariffs drove voter anger and could be contested between Trump and the new Congress, where some Republicans might vote to overturn them.

Appointees and Fed: the Republican-led Congress has under 30 days left, so confirming judges, cabinet members and appointees will be hard. Powell and other FOMC members may resign early, which would make it harder to confirm very dovish replacements.

Financial conditions: the recent tech-led equity repricing has not spread to credit. The risk is a feedback loop where slower AI capex weakens investment and GDP, falling equities and wider spreads tighten financial conditions, and that weighs further on activity. That is how an AI correction becomes a macro story.
The report has struggled with the idea of a meaningful Fed hiking cycle. If markets tighten financial conditions, several hikes become hard to deliver.

In a major drawdown, the report thinks both the Fed put and the Trump put are lower than markets assume. Inflation is unresolved, and Democrats may not treat the stock market as the same barometer of success. It may take considerably more pain to trigger either put.

Rates: the 10-year yield has fallen nearly 50bp, and the report's view that the economy cannot sustain rates above 5% has been vindicated. 5.3% on 10s was a good reloading point. The blue sweep should reinforce lower rates near term because divided government constrains fiscal spending and could stabilize Treasury issuance. Less incentive to escalate with Iran is a further tailwind for duration.

Longer term the bond outlook is less constructive. A higher chance of unified Democratic government in 2028 could bring heavier fiscal spending and issuance concerns, keeping curves steep. The report is slightly bullish at current levels but sees a return to sub-4% yields as difficult without a recession.

Equities: AI-related industries are the key risk. Democratic wins raise the chance of tighter AI and datacenter regulation and tax changes, such as compute-based taxes and local tax increases. The buildout may slow while valuation, positioning and AI financing concerns are in the background.

The report argues a slower pace of AI capex growth is enough to hurt, with no collapse needed. Profitability was never the vulnerability, concentration was. The post-election rally looks like position squaring, not the start of a sustained move. Stated stance: buy dips in bonds and sell rips in stocks.
